title: 7 Best LLMs for coding in April 2026
summary: Compare the best LLMs for coding in 2026 by SWE-bench Pro, price, and context window, across proprietary, open-weight, and local models.
body_markdown:
Ask three engineers on your team which model is the best LLM for code and you get three answers. Each one cites a different leaderboard, and each leaderboard ranks the models differently. One trusts a system card, one an aggregator index, and one whichever model fixed their bug last week.


OpenAI stopped reporting the benchmark most comparisons relied on. Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google then shipped new flagship or near-flagship models within four weeks of each other in September. A comparison written in April no longer matches today's models or prices.


Picture the budget review. Your pull request (PR) review agent was tuned on Claude Opus 5 in July. Opus 5.5 now costs less per token and scores higher. GPT-6.1 Sol undercuts both, and your finance lead asks why the model bill rose. Nobody re-ran the comparison, so nobody can answer.


This guide is for engineering leaders picking the best AI models for coding in 2026. It compares benchmarks, prices, context windows, and best fit, and covers what changes when AI-generated code runs in production.


**TL;DR**


- In BenchLM's third-party coding LLM ranking, Claude[Sonnet 5.5 sits first](https://benchlm.ai/coding) , Opus 5.5 second, and Fable 5.1 third.
- SWE-bench Verified no longer separates frontier models. Compare on SWE-bench Pro and a version-labeled Terminal-Bench, then test on your own repository.
- Mid-tier models cover most coding work. OpenAI says GPT-6.1 Sol[nearly matches GPT-6 Astra](https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-6-1-sol) on agentic coding at one-fifth the cost.
- GLM-5.2 lands within 3 points of GPT-5.6 Sol on SWE-bench Pro. GLM-5.2, Kimi K2.6, and DeepSeek V4 suit cost-sensitive and self-hosted work.
- Model choice is half the decision. Isolation, resume latency, and cost routing decide whether a coding agent holds up in production.


## How we compared the best LLMs for coding


We compare each large language model for coding on SWE-bench Pro. Scale built it from[1,865 tasks](https://scale.com/blog/swe-bench-pro) across 41 repositories in four languages.[Epoch AI's review](https://epoch.ai/benchmarks/swe-bench-verified/review) rates SWE-bench Verified as contaminated, and OpenAI stopped reporting it on February 23, 2026. Scale released[SWE-Bench Pro V2](https://labs.scale.com/blog/swe-bench-pro-v2) on September 22, 2026, and Anthropic's Opus 5.5 figure, for one, carries no edition label.


Most Pro scores here are vendor self-reported. We pair them with BenchLM's third-party aggregate and flag unconfirmed figures. Prices are list prices as of October 5, 2026, when we last updated this article.

Among the top coding models, SWE-bench Pro scores cluster between 53 and 90. Harness and edition explain part of that spread. Prices span more than ten-fold, from Gemini 3.8 Flash's promotional rate to Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra. Price should drive your shortlist more than score, so the sections below default to mid-tier models.


## Best proprietary LLMs for coding


Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google each ship frontier coding models, and each now sells a cheaper sibling that covers most daily work.


### Claude Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 for multi-file and long-running work


Pay for Opus 5.5 only where a failed run costs more than the tokens. In practice that means multi-file refactors and multi-hour agent runs where a restart wastes more than the token bill. Anthropic's Opus 5.5 page says it matches Fable 5.1 performance at 40% lower cost than Opus 5. That is Anthropic's cost-at-performance measure; the list price itself fell 20%, from 5/25. Sonnet 5.5 costs half as much with the same context and output limits. We found no Anthropic-published Sonnet 5.5 coding benchmarks, yet BenchLM's third-party index places it first. For daily work, start your team on Sonnet.


Opus 5.5's Pro score carries no edition label and no independent confirmation yet. Fable 5.1 lists at 2.5 times Opus 5.5's price yet ranks below it on BenchLM, so reserve it for the hardest long-horizon tasks.


### GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra for tool-heavy agent work


GPT-6 Astra is OpenAI's premium tier, released[September 3](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/changelog) . It pays for itself only when it removes retries, review cycles, or human time. We found no OpenAI-published SWE-bench Pro score for Astra. The only Astra Terminal-Bench 4.0 figure we found is in Anthropic's comparison table.


GPT-6.1 Sol followed on September 29 at 2/10 on its short-context tier, the same list price as Sonnet 5.5. OpenAI's claim that Sol nearly matches Astra has no outside confirmation yet. GPT-5.6 Sol remains the best-documented OpenAI model, and a July price cut made it cheaper. GPT-6.1 Sol's lower price leaves room for several retries before it costs as much as one Astra run. Until outside numbers arrive, start agent loops on GPT-6.1 Sol and escalate to Astra.


### Gemini 4 Argon and Gemini 3.8 Flash for large inputs


Google announced[Gemini 4 Argon](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/gemini-4-argon) and describes it as rolling out soon. We found no independent coding scores, so treat Argon as a model to evaluate, not to deploy. Google's Flash announcement says the Gemini 3.8 Flash price rises to 1.50/7.50 after December 31, 2026. Google calls it its best reasoning and coding model yet, though its coding results appear only as charts.


Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview is the newest Pro-tier model with published scores. Choose Gemini for multimodal and large-input work, and Claude or OpenAI for long agent loops until Argon has outside numbers.


## Best open-weight LLMs for coding


Open-weight models let you self-host, fine-tune, and skip per-token markups. The best open source coding LLM options now post SWE-bench Pro scores near GPT-5.6 Sol.


### Kimi K3, GLM-5.3, and GLM-5.2: the open models closest to the frontier


Among open models with first-party cards we verified, GLM-5.2 holds the best SWE-bench Pro score, close behind GPT-5.6 Sol. GLM-5.2's model card lists 743B parameters, a 1M context, and an MIT license. GLM-5.3 has since appeared, but the model-card numbers we can verify are for 5.2.


Moonshot's[Kimi K3 docs](https://platform.moonshot.ai/docs/guide/kimi-k3-quickstart) give a 1M context with no length tiering. First-party scores and dollar pricing weren't on the pages we retrieved. Kimi K2.6's model card lists 1T parameters with 32B active and a Modified MIT license. These aren't single-GPU models; K2.6 needs hundreds of gigabytes of memory to run locally. Use them through a hosted API or your own GPU cluster. Moonshot is China-based, so regulated teams should run a data-governance review before using its hosted API.


### DeepSeek V4 for low cost per task


DeepSeek V4 is a low-cost route to a frontier-adjacent model for bulk work. In DeepSeek's[V4 preview](https://www.deepseek.com/en/news/v4-preview) on April 24, 2026, V4-Pro runs 1.6T parameters with 49B active and V4-Flash 284B with 13B active, so self-hosting either typically needs a multi-GPU cluster. The API offers 1M context with 384K output and prices by peak and off-peak hours. DeepSeek's pricing page lists cache hits on v4-pro at $0.022 off-peak and $0.044 peak per million tokens. Coding agents resend the same repository prefix every step, so cache pricing likely matters most.


DeepSeek hasn't published a first-party SWE-bench Pro score we can verify. Third-party listings put V4 well below the closed leaders on SWE-bench Pro. Use it for code review, static analysis, and bulk transformations, after confirming V4's license on its model card and adding the hosted API's Chinese jurisdiction to your data-governance review.


### Best local LLM for coding


Qwen3-Coder-Next is our pick for the best local LLM for coding in 2026 on workstation-class hardware, chosen for efficiency rather than absolute score. It runs[80B total parameters](https://qwen.ai/blog?id=qwen3-coder-next) with 3B active and carries a 256K context under Apache 2.0. The Ollama build weighs about[52GB](https://ollama.com/library/qwen3-coder-next) and also runs in LM Studio or llama.cpp. It needs workstation-class memory rather than one consumer card.


For a single consumer GPU, Qwen3.6-27B is the pick: a dense 27B model whose quantized build fits in[18GB](https://ollama.com/library/qwen3.6) . Qwen3.6-27B trails Opus 5.5 by more than 30 points on Pro. Local models fit privacy-bound codebases, not autonomous multi-hour refactors.


## How to choose the best LLM for your coding workflow


Which LLM is best for coding at your company? The cheapest one that passes your eval, and that differs by workload.


- **Daily IDE work:** Start with Claude Sonnet 5.5 or GPT-6.1 Sol. Both list at mid-tier prices and suit the code generation and edits that make up most daily requests.
- **Long-horizon agents:** Start with Claude Opus 5.5. Escalate to Fable 5.1 or GPT-6 Astra only when one failed multi-hour run costs more than the price gap.
- **High-volume, cost-sensitive jobs:** Run Gemini 3.8 Flash, DeepSeek V4, or GLM-5.2 through a hosted API. Use each provider's batch tier where offered.
- **Regulated or self-hosted:** Run GLM-5.2 or Kimi K2.6 on your own GPUs, which removes the hosted-API governance question.
- **Local:** Use Qwen3.6-27B on one 24GB-class GPU, or Qwen3-Coder-Next if you have workstation memory. Both keep code on your own hardware.


Compare cost per completed task, not per token. Anthropic's Opus 5.5 system card prices CursorBench 4.0 runs. Fable 5.1 scored 51.8% at[$17.28 per task](https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/fc1b44717c85dc068bc6ba5024219938094694bd/Claude%20Opus%205.5%20System%20Card.pdf) , Opus 5 46.6% at $11.95, and GPT-5.6 Sol 41.7% at $8.23. Opus 5.5 beat all three at 57.8% on max effort. A cheaper model that fails often can cost more per merged change than a pricier one.


## How to evaluate coding LLMs on your own codebase


A benchmark pass isn't a mergeable PR. METR scored Claude 3.7 Sonnet patches against maintainer-written tests. An[average of 38%](https://metr.org/blog/2025-08-12-research-update-towards-reconciling-slowdown-with-time-horizons) passed, and none of the reviewed PRs were mergeable as-is. Vendor leaderboards measure test passage under a specific scaffold, so your own eval is the only number that transfers.


Build one from 20 to 50 of your merged PRs. For each, take the issue text, the pre-merge commit, and the tests the PR added. Run each candidate once under one harness and report pass@1; the[HumanEval pass@k problem](https://blaxel.ai/blog/humaneval-benchmark) applies to agents too. Log tokens, wall-clock time, and tool calls per task so cost per completed task falls out of the same run. SWE-bench Verified and LiveCodeBench are Python-only. They help you find the best LLM for programming in Python, but TypeScript or Go teams get no language-matched signal.


Keep human review gates regardless of the winner.[Stack Overflow's 2025 survey](https://survey.stackoverflow.co/2025) found more developers distrust AI tool accuracy than trust it. Track acceptance rate per model; that metric tells you when a cheaper model has caught up.


## What changes when AI-generated code runs in production


The model that wins your eval still writes code you can't run on shared infrastructure. Anthropic's[Claude Code sandboxing](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/claude-code-sandboxing) post calls for filesystem and network isolation. Without both, a compromised agent can exfiltrate keys or escape its environment. OpenAI tells[Agents SDK users](https://openai.com/index/the-next-evolution-of-the-agents-sdk) to keep credentials out of code-execution environments. For agents that execute AI-generated code, that means microVMs rather than containers, because containers share the host kernel.


Latency comes next. Agent infrastructure platforms like[Blaxel](https://blaxel.ai/platform/sandboxes) keep sandboxes in standby indefinitely at zero compute cost. They resume in under 25ms with filesystem and memory intact. Blaxel is a first-class sandbox provider in the OpenAI Agents SDK. One[arXiv analysis](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.28919v2) of harness economics traced $198,000 of monthly savings to picking the cheapest capable model per session. Misroutes took back $53,000. Measure misroutes before trusting the savings.

## FAQs


### What is the best LLM for coding right now?


Sonnet 5.5 is the default we'd start with. BenchLM's third-party index ranks it first, and it lists at half Opus 5.5's price. GPT-6.1 Sol matches that price, though its near-Astra claim is OpenAI's own and lacks outside confirmation. Add Opus 5.5 for long-running agents. Rankings shift within a quarter, so the best LLM for code generation on your team is whichever passes an eval built from your own merged PRs.


### What is the best open-source LLM for coding?


Among open models with first-party model cards, GLM-5.2 holds the best SWE-bench Pro score, under an MIT license. GLM-5.2, Kimi K2.6, and DeepSeek V4-Pro need multi-GPU hosting at their size. For a single consumer GPU, Qwen3.6-27B is the best open source LLM for coding in 2026 under Apache 2.0. Most of these are open-weight rather than Open Source Initiative (OSI) open source. Check the license before fine-tuning for a commercial product.


### Is SWE-bench Verified still reliable?


No, not as a differentiator between frontier models. As the methodology section notes, it is contaminated. Anthropic's own[Fable 5 system card](https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/d00db56fa754a1b115b6dd7cb2e3c342ee809620.pdf) reports 95%. Use SWE-bench Pro, which covers four languages and includes held-out and commercial repositories. Read any Terminal-Bench number alongside its version, then test on your own merged PRs.


### How do I reduce LLM costs for coding agents?


Route by task: send completions and small edits to Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol, or Gemini 3.8 Flash, and reserve Opus 5.5 for multi-file work. Keep agent prompts under the long-context thresholds. GPT-5.6 Sol and Gemini 3.1 Pro both raise rates above them. Use prompt caching and batch tiers wherever offered, since resent input tokens dominate coding agent traffic. Measure cost per completed task per model, and move work down a tier whenever acceptance rates hold.
